pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic: The inverse relationship between addition and subtraction — addition and subtraction 'undo' each other, so a known sum yields three related facts and a subtraction can be checked by adding back. Ages 6–7, building on unknown-addend and fact families.
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics): Y2 'recognise and use the inverse relationship between addition and subtraction and use this to check calculations and solve missing number problems'. Reappears in KS2 for checking with larger numbers.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): builds on 1.OA.4 (subtraction as unknown addend) and 1.OA.6 relationships; supports 2.NBT/3.NBT checking by inverse. Inverse operations are the explicit mechanism for solving □ + 9 = 14 and verifying answers.
• Operational details: teach through the fact family / part-whole triangle — one whole and two parts generate 2 additions and 2 subtractions. Use inverse deliberately for TWO jobs: (a) checking (15 + 7 = 22, so 22 − 7 should give 15) and (b) solving missing-number equations (□ + 9 = 14 → □ = 14 − 9). Emphasise it is a relationship between operations, not a new procedure.
• Checkpoint: Tier A (age 6) — given 6 + 4 = 10 states 10 − 4 = 6 and 10 − 6 = 4. Tier B (age 7) — solves □ + 9 = 14 by subtracting and checks a subtraction by adding back. Tier C (age 7+) — explains that addition undoes subtraction and uses inverse to check a calculation with two-digit numbers.
bestPractices: Anchor on the fact-family triangle / part-whole model so all four related facts come from one whole and two parts.
Make 'checking by the inverse' a routine habit after every calculation, not an add-on.
Use inverse explicitly to convert a missing-number equation into a calculation the child can do (□ + 9 = 14 → 14 − 9).
Keep the SAME three numbers while flipping the operation, so the child sees one relationship rather than four separate facts.
Contrast with situations where inverse reasoning is misapplied, e.g. reminding that order matters in the subtraction facts (10 − 6 vs 6 − 10).
keyRepresentations: Fact-family / part-whole triangle (one whole, two parts, four facts)
Bar model with the whole and two parts, read as add or subtract
Empty number line showing a forward jump and its reversing backward jump
Balance model where adding then subtracting the same amount returns to start
Cuisenaire rods showing a+b and the reverse whole−a
commonMisconceptions: Treating the four fact-family facts as unrelated things to memorise separately.
Believing subtraction facts can also be reversed freely (10 − 6 = 6 − 10), over-extending the 'undo' idea.
Checking a sum by repeating the SAME operation rather than using the inverse.
Solving □ + 9 = 14 by adding 9 and 14, not recognising subtraction as the inverse move.
Thinking 'undoing' requires a different, brand-new procedure rather than the operation they already know.

learn.summary: Help 6–7 year-olds see that addition and subtraction undo each other, so one known sum (e.g. 15 + 7 = 22) generates all four related facts, lets you check a calculation by reversing it, and lets you solve a missing-number equation (□ + 9 = 14) by subtracting. The core aim is to treat these as ONE relationship between operations, not four separate facts to memorise. Builds on fact families and part-whole/unknown-addend ideas.

activities.title: Do and undo it on a number line (with a fact-family triangle)
feedback: If the learner recomputes the subtraction from scratch, point back to the triangle: the whole (22) and two parts (15, 7) already give the subtraction — read it off rather than counting again.
If the learner writes 15 − 7 = 22 or similar, mark on the bar/triangle which number is the whole: you can only take a part away FROM the whole, and 15 and 7 are both parts.

If the learner checks 15 + 7 = 22 by just adding 15 + 7 again, point out that repeating the same calculation can repeat the same mistake. Reversing it (22 − 7 = 15) is a real check, in the same way that adding the parts back (15 + 7) checks the subtraction 22 − 7 = 15.
When the backward jump lands exactly on 15, name it: 'the subtraction undid the addition.'
activities.rationale: A reversible forward/backward action makes 'undo' literal and ties all four facts to a single whole-and-parts structure, directly targeting the misconception that related facts are unrelated. The number-line and triangle are one way to realise this; equivalent reversing can be shown on paper, on a balance model, or with Cuisenaire rods, and none of these media is required over the others.
sourceClaims: Y2 pupils recognise and use the inverse relationship between addition and subtraction to check calculations and solve missing-number problems.
Fact families and the inverse relationship are taught via part-whole structures; children commonly treat related facts as separate and check by repeating rather than reversing.
learnerActions: Start at 15 on a number line and make a forward jump of +7, landing on 22.
Before reversing, predict out loud where a backward jump of 7 will land and why.
Make the backward jump of −7 and confirm you return exactly to 15.
Say in your own words why the subtraction lands back on the start: it is the same jump run in reverse.
Fill in a fact-family triangle with the whole (22) and the two parts (15 and 7), then write all four facts: 15 + 7 = 22, 7 + 15 = 22, 22 − 7 = 15, 22 − 15 = 7.
Check a subtraction by adding the parts back: verify 22 − 7 = 15 by computing 15 + 7.

(Optional) Show the same reversing with another model: a balance that returns to its start after you add then subtract the same amount, or Cuisenaire rods laid as 15 + 7 and then the whole with one part removed.
activities.intendedInsight: Subtraction reverses addition over the SAME three numbers, so taking one part from the whole returns the other part; one sum gives four related facts and a built-in way to check.

activities.title: Solve a missing number by reversing
feedback: If the learner adds 9 and 14, remind them that the box plus 9 already makes 14, so you need to take 9 away from 14 to find the box.
Praise a correct check that substitutes the answer back into the original equation (5 + 9 = 14).
activities.rationale: Turning the equation into a doable subtraction shows inverse operations as the mechanism for solving, not a brand-new procedure.
sourceClaims: Y2 pupils recognise and use the inverse relationship between addition and subtraction to check calculations and solve missing-number problems.
Understanding subtraction as an unknown addend (1.OA.4) and part-whole/fact-family relationships underpins using inverse operations to solve and check.
learnerActions: Look at □ + 9 = 14 and decide what operation would find the missing part.
Explain why subtracting (14 − 9) finds the box: addition and subtraction undo each other.
Compute □ = 14 − 9 = 5 and check by putting it back: 5 + 9 = 14.
Try one or two more missing-number equations, each solved by the inverse and then checked by adding back.
activities.intendedInsight: A missing-addend equation becomes a calculation you can already do by using the inverse operation, and the answer can be confirmed by reversing again.

activities.title: Explain WHY adding back proves a subtraction
feedback: If the learner says 15 − 7 = 22, steer to the whole: 22 is the whole; you subtract a part from the whole, so valid subtractions are 22 − 7 and 22 − 15.
If the learner only recites facts without saying the operations undo each other, ask them to point to the jump that reverses the addition.
Accept a justification that names 22 as the whole and explains the returned part.
activities.rationale: A justification prompt exercises the conceptual 'explain' goal and lets a learner confront the over-generalisation that any pair of the three numbers reverses.
sourceClaims: Fact families and the inverse relationship are taught via part-whole structures; children commonly treat related facts as separate and check by repeating rather than reversing.
learnerActions: Given 22 − 7 = 15, explain how you could be sure it is right WITHOUT redoing the subtraction.
Discuss the difference between reversing (adding the parts back) and simply repeating the same subtraction.
Respond to the claim that 'subtraction undoes too, so 15 − 7 = 22' and explain why that is wrong using which number is the whole.
State a DIFFERENT true subtraction from the same three numbers (22 − 15 = 7) and justify it.
activities.intendedInsight: Checking works because addition reverses subtraction over the same whole and parts; the 'undo' idea applies to taking a part from the whole, not to any rearrangement of the three numbers.

activities.title: Match and consolidate related facts
feedback: For a choice that repeats 15 + 7, explain that a genuine check reverses the operation; an inverse check is 22 − 7 = 15 (or 22 − 15 = 7).
For a mismatched subtraction, return to the whole-and-parts triangle.
activities.rationale: Recognition and fill-in tasks consolidate the four related facts and the inverse check; on their own they confirm familiarity but recognition alone does not require the learner to produce and feel the do-and-undo action.
learnerActions: Match one sum (15 + 7 = 22) to its three related facts.
Fill in blanks in missing-number equations such as □ + 9 = 14, solving by the inverse.
Choose which calculation correctly checks 15 + 7 = 22, distinguishing an inverse check (22 − 7 = 15 or 22 − 15 = 7) from a decoy that just repeats the same addition.
activities.intendedInsight: Fluent recall and recognition of the four related facts and the correct inverse check, reinforcing the single relationship.

constraints: Keep the SAME three numbers while flipping the operation so the learner sees one relationship, not four isolated facts.
Make 'check by the inverse' a routine habit after calculating, in line with the objective, rather than an optional afterthought.

Distinguish the whole from the parts explicitly: subtractions take a part from the whole (22 − 7, 22 − 15); a part minus a part (15 − 7) is NOT one of this fact family's four facts (15 − 7 = 8 is a valid operation but a different problem).
Emphasise that subtraction does not reverse 'freely' — order matters, so do not over-extend the undo idea to 15 − 7 = 22.

A fixed/static fact-family picture with tappable corners can anchor the four facts and the checking idea, but it does not let the learner perform the reversing action; it can support rather than stand in for do-and-undo work.

Recognition and matching tasks can check recall of the four related facts and the correct inverse check, but recognition alone does not elicit independent production or the felt experience of reversing; pair them with reversing and explanation work rather than relying on them alone, without mandating a particular medium or strict ordering.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The source's correctAnswer field contains self-corrected scratch text ('22 − 6... no — 22 − 15 = 7'); the two valid related subtractions are 22 − 7 = 15 and 22 − 15 = 7. This rewrite uses only the corrected forms and never offers the scratch value as an option.

The original listed a '3D adds nothing' judgement for this numeric relationship; this is a catalog fit opinion, not an established pedagogical law, so it is omitted from learner-facing guidance. A third spatial dimension is simply not needed here, but no universal-necessity claim is made either way.
Two source claims (CCSS-M grade 1; Carpenter et al. CGI) were marked unverified in the original; retained as cited where they support a principle, without upgrading their confidence.

The interactive number-line/triangle, 'undo'/'check' controls, tappable corners, linked panes, balance model, and Cuisenaire rods are optional concrete examples of the same reversing mechanism, not mandatory tooling; the reversing and checking can equally be done on paper. No claim is made that any one medium teaches this better than another.

assess.poeTask: Predict what happens if you start at 15, jump forward 7 on a number line, then jump back 7. Say where you'll land and why BEFORE you move. Then do it — what does landing back on 15 tell you about how adding and subtracting 7 are related?
probeDeeper: Why does taking 7 away from 22 have to give 15 back?
Which of your three numbers is the whole, and how does that decide the subtractions?
If I made a mistake and wrote 22 − 7 = 16, how would the inverse show me I was wrong?
Can you also make a DIFFERENT true subtraction from these three numbers? What is it?
assess.correctAnswer: 22 − 7 = 15 (or 22 − 6... no — 22 − 15 = 7). Either 22 − 7 = 15 or 22 − 15 = 7. Explanation: subtraction undoes addition, so taking back one part from the whole must return the other part — the three numbers form one whole (22) and two parts (15 and 7).

errorPatterns.pattern: Treats the facts as separate — recomputes a subtraction from scratch rather than reading it off the relationship.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Use the fact-family triangle: one whole and two parts generate all four facts; practise reading them off without recalculating.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Starts counting/calculating a subtraction instead of deriving it from 15 + 7 = 22.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'Subtraction undoes too, so 15 − 7 also works' — over-extends reversal and offers an invalid subtraction from the wrong pair.
errorPatterns.nextMove: On the bar model, mark which number is the whole (22) — you can only take a part FROM the whole; 15 and 7 are both parts.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Gives 15 − 7 = 22 or similar, subtracting a part from a part or expecting the whole as the answer.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'To check it, do 15 + 7 again' — checks by repeating the same operation rather than the inverse.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Contrast repeating (same errors reappear) with reversing; establish adding-back as the check.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: When asked to check, re-adds the two numbers instead of subtracting.

responseLevels.gap: Cannot produce a valid related subtraction, or recomputes with no sense of relationship; may give 15 − 7.
responseLevels.full: States a valid subtraction, identifies 22 as the whole, and justifies it by inverse reasoning ('subtraction undoes addition, so the part comes back'), and can use it to check or solve a missing-number equation.
responseLevels.partial: Produces a correct related subtraction but justifies it by calculating, or lists the facts without saying the operations undo each other; doesn't reliably identify the whole.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: I worked out that 15 + 7 = 22. Using only those three numbers, tell me a subtraction that must also be true — and explain how you know it is true without working it out from scratch.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who has memorised facts separately, or who thinks checking means redoing, will either recompute or offer an invalid rearrangement (e.g. 15 − 7). A child who holds the inverse relationship names a valid subtraction immediately and justifies it by 'undoing' rather than by calculating — the 'without working it out' clause is what forces the relational justification.
